attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter, stated as fact.

semantics.note: Keeps all three parts: Microsoft was the only one, its last disclosure was in January 2025, and it never disclosed again. Leaving out the monthly conversion in the parenthetical is fine.

contract.note: Counting a quantified dollar band such as 'multi-billion dollar run rate' as talking about AI revenue is an ordinary reading. Zitron himself accepts a run rate as AI revenue. The result depends on that reading, and the reading is fair.

evidence.note: Microsoft's January 29, 2025 earnings remarks confirm the $13B AI run rate. This confirms the January 2025 part but not the uniqueness or the 'never again' part.
In its April 2024 earnings call, before Microsoft's statement, Amazon described a multi-billion dollar AI revenue run rate. This is another hyperscaler disclosing AI revenue.

In October 2025, Alphabet said its enterprise AI products generate billions in quarterly revenue. This is realized rather than annualized revenue, so it counts only as context under the contract's metric. It still points the same way.

reviews.rationale: The contradiction condition is met. Amazon's April 2024 primary disclosure of a multi-billion dollar AI revenue run rate shows Microsoft was not the only hyperscaler to talk about AI revenue. Alphabet's October 2025 statement reinforces this. The January 2025 Microsoft statement does hold. Whether Microsoft ever disclosed again is not settled by the packet. The central uniqueness claim fails.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter.

semantics.note: An unqualified 'will be very, very difficult' and 'near-impossible' make this a scored forecast with no deadline. The context points to Anthropic and OpenAI subscribers.

contract.note: The plain reading (strong subscriber resistance to substantial price increases, little lasting move to API billing) matches the words. 'Very difficult' has no threshold, but the reading is not stretched for or against the speaker.

evidence.note: A September 2026 TechRadar opinion piece reports billing changes, such as metered agentic usage and enterprise seats being retired. It has no data on retention or acceptance and concerns enterprise customers rather than consumers.

reviews.rationale: The forecast has no deadline, and the packet has no conclusive event. That would need representative cohort data on retention or API conversion after an implemented change. The only item reports billing changes without showing how subscribers responded, so the outcome is unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter.

semantics.note: Keeps 'burning', the superlative, and his TARP and PPP figures. The opening 'Even if you are impressed' framing is rhetorical and dropping it is fine.

contract.note: Reading 'burning' as cumulative gross LLM spending incurred by the post date is fair given the context. Testing the named program comparisons separately from the literal superlative is reasonable.

evidence.note: Amazon's 2025 increase in capex, attributed mainly to AI, plus a planned 2026 figure. This is one company's yearly change, not a cumulative industry total of LLM spending.
GAO puts PPP commitment authority at about $814B and lending at about $800B. This is the benchmark's scale; it says nothing about AI spending.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no reconciled, non-duplicated total of actual cumulative LLM spending by March 17, 2026. It also does not separate LLM spending from general infrastructure spending or from planned spending. Without that, neither the TARP/PPP comparison nor the broader superlative can be settled.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter.

semantics.note: A causal claim: unpredictable token use makes any budgeting a non-starter. Adding 'metered usage' matches the context, which imagines a switch to API billing.

contract.note: Zitron's absolute wording ('no way', 'any kind of budgeting') makes it fair to count estimates and spending caps as budgeting. The result depends on that reading. His narrower point, about fixed-cost completion for consumers, is not what he literally said.

evidence.note: Anthropic documented per-workspace monthly API spend limits in September 2024, before the post. That is a form of budgeting, though it does not guarantee a task finishes within budget.
A February 2025 developer-set thinking budget gives control over one source of variable token use. It does not predict a whole task's cost.

A November 2025 preprint shows advance cost estimates producing useful benchmark results with rare budget overruns. It also concedes cost is non-deterministic, and it covers benchmarks, not consumer coding.

reviews.rationale: Before the post, spend caps, thinking budgets, and estimate-based budgeting that kept useful work within budget were all available. This contradicts 'no way to anticipate' and 'any kind of budgeting a non-starter' under the contract's reading. The narrower point holds: exact per-prompt token use is non-deterministic, and caps do not guarantee completion.
